newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's rival Moslem bodies plan unity congress.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's rival Moslem bodies plan unity congress.

text.p: Bulgaria's two rival Moslem leaders agreed on Wednesday to hold a joint conference in September aiming to unite their religious councils under a new leader.

"Nadim Gendzhev and Fikri Sali, heads of the two Moslem Councils, signed today a declaration for holding a joint conference to unite the two bodies," Georgi Krastev of the government's Ecclesiastical Directorate told Reuters.
The meeting, the first between the two rival Moslem leaders in five years, has been mediated by the Directorate.
Sali, head of the High Moslem Council, has repeatedly urged the country's new reformist government to reverse a decision of the former Socialist rulers and register his religious council.
The Supreme Court in March overturned a decision by the former Socialist cabinet to refuse to register Sali's Council as Bulgaria's highest Moslem body.
Sali was chief mufti from 1992 to November 1994, when a national council elected Nedim Gendjev as head of the High Spiritual Council and appointed a new chief mufti.

In March 1995, more than 1,000 Moslems voted at a special national conference to restore Sali following allegations that Gendjev had once been an agent of the political department of the communist secret services.
Calling themselves the High Moslem Council, they sought registration from the Socialist government, which refused on the grounds that it had already registered a Moslem council.

Gendjev was appointed chief mufti in 1988, a year before communist ruler Todor Zhivkov was toppled. During the 1980s, one million ethnic Turks were forced to adopt Bulgarian names and their religious and human rights were severely curbed.
Their rights were restored after Zhivkov's overthrow and many of those who left for Turkey have since returned.

Directorate sources said Deputy Prime Minister Vesselin Metodiev, who was present at the meeting, had urged both Gendjev and Sali to step down and agree on a new leader who would unite Bulgarian Moslems.

The dispute between Bulgaria's two Moslem authorities mirrors a longstanding row between the country's Orthodox Christians. The Supreme Court on March 5 declared invalid the registration of one of two rival synods of the Orthodox church.
